```{r}
source("R/helpers.R")
set.seed(STUDENT_SEED)

population_mean <- 0
population_sd <- 1
generator <- function(sample_size) {
  rnorm(sample_size, mean = population_mean, sd = population_sd)
}
```

## Question and prediction

The population is already normal, so I expect the sampling distribution of the
sample mean to look approximately normal even for relatively small sample
sizes. The theoretical mean is `r population_mean` and the theoretical standard
deviation is `r population_sd`.

## Original population

```{r}
population <- rnorm(10000, mean = population_mean, sd = population_sd)
plot_population_histogram(population, "Original Standard Normal population", "Population value")
```

The original population is continuous, symmetric, and bell-shaped. Its mean
and standard deviation are known from the model rather than estimated from one
small sample.

## Simulation method

For each sample size, I generated 10,000 independent samples and calculated the
mean of each sample. The sample sizes were 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, and 200.

```{r}
means_by_size <- simulate_sample_means(generator)
summary_table <- summarize_sample_means(
  means_by_size,
  theoretical_mean = population_mean,
  theoretical_sd = population_sd
)
print_summary(summary_table)
first_screened_n <- summary_table$sample_size[summary_table$screening_rule][1]
chosen_row <- summary_table[summary_table$sample_size == first_screened_n, , drop = FALSE]
```

## Sample sizes investigated

I investigated sample sizes `n = 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, and 200`. I started
with small samples to see whether normality was already present, included
`n = 30` because it is a common classroom rule, and went up to 200 to see what
happened for larger samples.

The theoretical standard error for a sample of size `n` is

$$SE(\bar X) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}.$$

The simulated standard deviations should be close to that formula. The
sampling distributions should also stay centered near zero.

## Visual evidence

```{r}
selected_sizes <- c(2, 10, 30, 100)
plot_selected_diagnostics(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Standard Normal")
plot_selected_qq(means_by_size, selected_sizes, "Standard Normal Q-Q plot")
```

The histograms and Q-Q plots provide visual evidence about shape. Because the
original population is normal, increasing `n` mainly makes the sampling
distribution narrower; it does not need to wait for the CLT to create a bell
shape.

## Approximate normal decision

My final answer is **n =** `r first_screened_n`. At this sample size, the
histogram and Q-Q plot looked approximately normal, and the numerical checks
were also close to the normal reference values. The skewness was
`r round(chosen_row$skewness, 3)`, the excess kurtosis was
`r round(chosen_row$excess_kurtosis, 3)`, and the simulated standard deviation
was `r round(chosen_row$simulated_sd, 4)` compared with a theoretical standard
error of `r round(chosen_row$theoretical_se, 4)`.

This result makes sense because the original population is already normal.
Taking the mean of normal observations still gives a normal distribution.
Increasing `n` mainly makes the spread smaller.

## What surprised me

I was surprised that the sample means looked approximately normal even at the
smallest sample size. I expected the standard error to get smaller as `n`
increased, but I did not expect the bell shape to be present so quickly.
